Retirement

/rih-TY-er-ment/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Retirement means the act of leaving one's job or career, usually upon reaching a certain age.

After forty years of teaching chemistry, Mr. Alvarez announced his retirement at the spring assembly, to a standing ovation.

Worked Example

The shortstop's retirement ended a nineteen-year career; he joked that his knees had made the decision long before he did.

He is leaving his career permanently, at the natural end of his working years — not switching teams or taking a break. A permanent exit from a career, usually late in it, is the defining shape of retirement.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

departure: A departure is simply the act of leaving — any exit, from any place, for any reason. Retirement is one very specific departure: leaving paid work for good, usually at the natural end of a career. Every retirement is a departure; a departure could just be catching a train.

withdrawal: A withdrawal is a pulling back or out of an activity, and it can be partial or quiet — a candidate withdraws from a race. Retirement is a formal, permanent exit from working life itself, usually marked by age and a completed career. You can withdraw from one contest; retirement closes the whole game.

resignation: A resignation is formally giving up a position — often mid-career, and often to move on to something else. Retirement closes a working life at its natural end, with no next job implied. A rising manager resigns to join a rival; a veteran who leaves for good takes retirement.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

hiring: being taken on for a job

reinstatement: being restored to a position

Where it sits · how much is given up for good — sabbatical → retirement → abdication

sabbatical vs. retirement: A sabbatical is milder than retirement — the professor took a one-year sabbatical and returned to her lab afterward, career fully intact.

abdication vs. retirement: An abdication is more dramatic than a retirement — when the aging king abdicated, he gave up not just his daily work but a crown and a throne.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: back

Root — tire

Root — tire: to pull, to draw (French tirer)

Suffix — -ment

Suffix — -ment: result or process of

Put it together

Put it together: French retirer meant "to draw back" — re- (back) + tirer (to pull). Retirement is literally "the act of pulling oneself back" from working life. One honest caution: tirer's own deeper origin is uncertain, and it left almost no other everyday English words — so this root is a one-time story, not a pattern to hunt for elsewhere.

Use the root in a new word: tirade

Use the root in a new word: tirade: The coach launched into a tirade after the third fumble — a long speech "drawn out" at length, likely from the same Romance verb meaning "to pull."

Word Choice

Neutral / workplace

Retirement and employment bookend a working life: employment begins when you're hired, and retirement — a word you're also learning in this unit — marks the day you leave paid work for good. Retirement implies age or a completed career; leaving one job mid-career for another is a resignation, not a retirement.
